slides.title: The residual stream
slides.summary: Each layer reads the token vectors, computes something and adds the result back, so information builds up instead of being overwritten.
body: The most useful mental picture of a transformer: a wide stream of vectors, one per token, flows from the bottom of the model to the top.
Each layer has two parts, attention and an MLP. Each part reads the current stream, computes an update, and adds it back: x = x + f(x). Nothing is overwritten. Contributions pile up.

ul: Why it helps training: learning sends an error signal backwards through every layer. The plain addition gives that signal a direct path to the earliest layers, so even 100-layer models train reliably. This is called a residual or skip connection.
Why it helps the model think: each layer can make a small, targeted edit, such as adding "this word is a verb" or "this refers to Paris", which later layers can then read.

body.note: A shared document that every layer annotates. Nobody deletes earlier notes; each layer adds its own in the margin, and the final reader sees them all at once.

code: x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))   # read, write back

slides.title: Normalisation: LayerNorm and RMSNorm
slides.summary: Before each part of a layer, vectors are rescaled to a standard size so the numbers stay stable.
body: Every layer adds to the stream, so the numbers can grow larger and larger on the way up. Large, swinging values make training unstable.

So just before each attention or MLP part, a copy of the vector is normalised to a standard scale. Only the copy going into the sublayer is rescaled; the stream itself keeps its values. This placement is called pre-norm, and it's standard in modern LLMs. There are two common recipes:

ul: LayerNorm: subtract the average, divide by the standard deviation, then apply a learned scale and shift.
RMSNorm: skip the average and just divide by the root-mean-square, the typical size of the numbers. Slightly cheaper, works as well, and used by Llama and many others.

body: Try it: scale the input up ten times. The normalised output doesn't change at all.

body.note: Normalisation keeps each sublayer's input in a predictable range, however much has built up in the stream. It's a small step, but deep models don't train well without it.

slides.title: The MLP: where most parameters live
slides.summary: The MLP processes each token on its own. It holds most of the model's parameters and much of its stored knowledge.
body: Attention moves information between tokens. The MLP (multi-layer perceptron, also called the feed-forward network) then works on each token on its own, in three steps:

ul: Expand: multiply the vector up to a much wider size, typically about 4 × d.
Activate: pass every number through a simple curved function (shown on the right).
Project back: multiply back down to size d, ready to add to the stream.

body: About two-thirds of a model's parameters are in these MLPs. Research suggests they act partly like key-value memories for facts: a pattern meaning "Eiffel Tower" in the input switches on parts of the MLP that add "Paris" to the stream.

Two matrix multiplications in a row are equivalent to one. Without a bend in between, the whole model would collapse into a single linear function, however many layers it had. The curved activation function is what lets stacked layers represent complicated patterns. Modern models use smooth curves like GELU or SiLU, often in a gated form called SwiGLU.
code: def forward(self, x):          # x: [B, n, d]
return self.w2(h)                     # back to [B, n, d]

slides.title: Count the parameters yourself
slides.summary: You can estimate a model's size, and the memory it needs, from three numbers.
body: Each layer's weights come from a few matrices, so the parameter count is easy to estimate:

ul: Attention: four d × d matrices (Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo) = 4d².
So each layer has about 12d², and the whole model has about 12·N·d², plus V·d for the embedding table.

body.note: A 7B-class model has d = 4,096 and N = 32 layers: 12 × 32 × 4,096² ≈ 6.4 billion, plus about 0.1 billion for a 32k-token embedding table. Real designs differ a little (GQA, SwiGLU's three matrices), but the estimate lands close.

body: Each parameter is stored as a number of fixed size: 2 bytes in bf16 (the usual format), 1 byte at 8 bits, half a byte in 4-bit quantised formats. A 7B model needs about 14 GB in bf16 but only about 3.5 GB at 4 bits. That's how quantisation lets big models run on a laptop.
Try the presets, then move the sliders.

body.note: That's only the weights. Running the model also needs memory for the KV cache (see Output & inference), and training needs several times more again for gradients and optimiser state.

code: params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
# 7B params * 2 bytes = ~14 GB just to load in bf16

slides.title: Stack it N times
slides.summary: A model is the same layer design repeated many times, each copy with its own weights.
body: A full model is one block repeated N times: 32 layers for a typical 7–8B model, 80 or more for the largest open models. Every block has the same design, but each has its own learned weights.
Interpretability research finds rough tendencies in what different depths do:

ul: Early layers: local patterns and surface features, such as word pieces joining up into words.
Middle layers: more abstract features, like topic, meaning and relationships between things.
Late layers: turning all of that into a prediction for the next token.

body: These are tendencies, not hard boundaries.

body.note: Because every block maps [B, n, d] to [B, n, d], depth is just a config value. The main dials of the architecture are width (d), depth (N) and number of heads (h). Making a model bigger mostly means turning these up.

slides.title: Mixture of experts
slides.summary: Mixture-of-experts models have many MLPs per layer but use only a few for each token, so they're huge yet relatively cheap to run.
body: Many frontier models replace each layer's single MLP with a set of experts: several separate MLPs, plus a small router network. For each token, the router picks the top few experts (often 2, sometimes 8 out of more than 100) and blends their outputs.

ul: The benefit: total parameters, and with them knowledge capacity, grow a lot. Each token only runs through a few experts, so compute per token stays modest.
The cost: every expert has to sit in GPU memory, even when idle.
The catch: the router must be trained to spread work evenly. Otherwise it sends everything to a few favourites and the rest are wasted.

body: Pick different tokens on the right to see different experts light up.

body.note: "Expert" is a misleading name. Experts don't neatly specialise in subjects like "maths" or "French". What they learn to specialise in is usually much harder for people to interpret.

code: out = sum(w[..., i] * experts[idx[..., i]](x) for i in range(2))
